learning_objective: Write and run your first SELECT query to return a customer contact list

end_state.visual_summary: Open the Execute SQL tab, type the commented query SELECT FirstName, LastName, Email FROM Customer, run it with F5, and show the result pane with the contact list

narration_beats.text: In this video, we will write our first SELECT query to pull a clean customer contact list for WSDA Music management. We will add a comment header, list the columns, name the Customer table, and run the query.

We type a comment header at the top of the query so anyone who opens the file later can see who created it, when it was written, and what problem it solves. The header appears above the SQL and documents the query before any code runs, which is a professional habit worth keeping.

observed_state.summary: The Execute SQL tab is active, showing a SQL comment header with creator, date, and description, with no query results displayed yet.
observed_state.editor_content:
/*
Created By: WSDA Student
Create Date: 2026-08-31
Description: Customer contact list for management
*/

narration_beats.text: We type the SELECT clause, listing the columns FirstName, LastName, and Email. SELECT tells the database which columns to return, so we ask for only the contact fields we need. The SELECT clause appears between the comment header and the FROM clause, defining the output clearly.

observed_state.summary: The Execute SQL tab is active, showing a SQL query with a header comment and a SELECT statement for FirstName, LastName, and Email, with no results yet displayed.
observed_state.editor_content:
/*
Created By: WSDA Student
Create Date: 2026-08-31
Description: Customer contact list for management
*/
SELECT
  FirstName,
  LastName,
  Email

narration_beats.text: We type FROM Customer to name the data source for the columns. FROM tells the database which table holds the data, so the query knows to look in the Customer table. This completes the simplest useful query pattern, asking for specific data from one table.

observed_state.summary: The Execute SQL tab is active showing a query that selects FirstName, LastName, and Email from the Customer table, with no results displayed yet.
observed_state.editor_content:
/*
Created By: WSDA Student
Create Date: 2026-08-31
Description: Customer contact list for management
*/
SELECT
  FirstName,
  LastName,
  Email
FROM Customer;

narration_beats.text: We run the query by clicking the Execute SQL toolbar button. The result pane fills with the contact list, and the requested FirstName, LastName, and Email columns appear in the grid below the editor.

observed_state.summary: The Execute SQL tab shows a query selecting FirstName, LastName, and Email from the Customer table, with results displayed in a grid below and execution details in the log panel.

narration_beats.text: We see 60 rows returned in the result pane with FirstName, LastName, and Email headers for each customer. The row count confirms the contact list is complete, and the three requested columns match exactly what we named in the SELECT clause.

observed_state.summary: The Execute SQL tab shows a query selecting FirstName, LastName, and Email from the Customer table, with results displaying 60 rows returned successfully.

narration_beats.text: The result pane shows the complete customer contact list, with each customer record appearing once in the order it is stored. Management now has a reliable set of first names, last names, and email addresses without extra columns cluttering the view or slowing the report. This focused output is exactly what management requested.

Adding a comment header at the top of the query is a professional habit. It records who created the query, when it was written, and what problem it solves, which helps anyone who opens the file later. Good comments turn a quick one-off query into documentation the whole team can trust and maintain.

We have written our first SELECT query and pulled a complete customer contact list. The query returned only exactly the columns we needed and included a clear comment header. Next, we will make those column headers friendlier for management reports by using aliases.
